# UI/UX Preservation & Visual Stability Rules

### 1. Zero Unprompted UI Changes
- **NEVER alter, redesign, re-theme, re-style, or reorganize existing user interfaces without explicit instruction or approval from the user.**
- Do not change existing colors, themes, typography, layout structures, spacing, borders, shadows, component libraries, or visual hierarchy simply because you think a different design looks "better" or "more modern".
- Every existing screen, view, component, and widget is intentional. Treat existing visual implementations as strictly protected contracts.

### 2. Mandatory Approval Before Visual Redesigns
- If you believe an existing UI needs a redesign, or if a new feature requires significant changes to existing layouts, **you MUST ask the user for confirmation first** before modifying any existing visual code.
- Present proposed visual modifications or tradeoffs clearly in text/questions before altering any UI code.

### 3. Match Existing Design Systems & Aesthetic Exactly
- When building new components, screens, modals, or widgets:
  - Match the existing typography, color palette, design tokens, button styles, borders, and spacing system already established in the codebase.
  - Follow the existing component library and styling patterns (e.g., Tailwind classes, CSS modules, design tokens, component wrappers) without introducing conflicting design conventions or third-party styles.
  - Keep new additions seamless and indistinguishable in style from existing features.

### 4. Surgical UI Integration
- When adding new elements (e.g., a button, menu item, filter, or status indicator) into an existing view:
  - Integrate surgically without modifying or refactoring the surrounding layout, parent containers, adjacent components, or global styles.
  - Do not remove or reposition existing buttons, navigation links, controls, or data displays unless explicitly instructed.


# Zero-Regression Policy & Code Preservation Rules

### 1. Never Break Previously Working Functionality
- **The primary directive on every task is: do not break what already works.**
- Adding a new feature, fixing a bug, or extending existing code must never degrade, break, or disable existing features, flows, or edge cases.

### 2. Inspect and Understand Before Modifying
- Before editing existing files, inspect all relevant code paths, call sites, consumers, type definitions, and dependencies.
- Understand how data flows through the component or service before changing props, parameters, state shapes, or return values.
- Identify existing invariants, assumptions, and edge case handlers and ensure they remain satisfied.

### 3. Surgical, Minimal, and Additive Changes
- **Keep changes scoped strictly to what was requested.**
- Prefer additive implementations (e.g., adding an optional parameter or a new dedicated handler) rather than mutating existing core functions used across multiple features.
- Avoid large unsolicited refactors, file restructuring, or cleanup passes on working code during feature additions or targeted bug fixes.
- Do not remove existing logic, props, event listeners, or error handlers unless explicitly asked to deprecate or replace them.

### 4. Maintain Backward Compatibility
- Preserve existing component prop interfaces, function signatures, return types, API contracts, database schemas, and state shapes.
- If an existing function or component is modified, ensure all existing callers continue to work seamlessly without regressions.

### 5. Verification & Pre/Post-Flight Checks
- Verify both the **new functionality** AND the **existing functionality** that shares the modified code or context.
- Run existing test suites, linting, and typechecks before and after making changes.
- If automated tests are not available, mentally trace or manually verify all existing workflows connected to the modified files.

### 6. Mandatory Confirmation for Breaking Changes
- If a requested feature or fix inherently conflicts with existing behavior or requires breaking an existing contract, **stop and ask the user for confirmation** before proceeding.


# Search Tool Configuration

## Default Search Tool: rgrep

All AI agents and shell commands must use `rgrep` (ripgrep) instead of `grep` as the default search tool.

- `rgrep` is a symlink to `rg` (ripgrep 15.2.0) located at `/home/rover/.local/bin/rgrep`
- `rgrep` is faster than `grep` and provides better default behavior
- All shell configurations (fish, bash, zsh) alias `grep` to `rgrep`

### Agent-Specific Configuration
- **OpenCode**: Configured to use `rgrep` via shell alias
- **Claude**: Uses `rgrep` via shell alias
- **Antigravity**: Uses `rgrep` via shell alias
- **Zed**: Uses `rgrep` via shell alias
- **Cursor**: Uses `rgrep` via shell alias
- **Codex**: Uses `rgrep` via shell alias

### Shell Aliases
- `alias grep='rgrep'` in fish, bash, and zsh configurations
- `rgrep --version` confirms ripgrep 15.2.0 is active


# Neural Model Training & Checkpoint Continuity Standards

### 1. Checkpoint Continuity & Fine-Tuning
- **Never discard learned model representations by default**:
  - Training commands must support `--checkpoint <path>` or `--resume` to allow fine-tuning and progressive learning.
  - Subsequent training runs should build on top of validated best checkpoints (e.g. continuing from 66%+ with a calibrated lower learning rate such as 5e-5 or 1e-4) rather than forcing a random-weights cold start.
  - Cold starts should only occur if explicitly instructed or if architectural changes fundamentally invalidate the tensor shapes.

### 2. Checkpoint Preservation Guarantee
- Training loops must never overwrite a superior checkpoint with an inferior one during gradient descent fluctuations.
- A new best checkpoint file must only be saved when validation calibration or accuracy strictly improves.


# Stella Decision Coprocessor & Safety Copilot Rules

### 1. Mandatory Safety Gating for Irreversible Actions
- Before executing potentially destructive, dangerous, or irreversible actions (such as `git push --force`, `rm -rf`, dropping tables, permanent file deletions, system modifications), the agent **must** verify safety invariants through Stella's safety veto engine (`should_proceed` tool or `~/.local/bin/stella_mcp`).
- If Stella's veto layer returns `Blocked`, the agent must NOT execute the destructive command unless an explicit user override with justification is provided.

### 2. Fast Patch Ranking
- When evaluating multiple alternative code fixes, refactorings, or candidate diffs, call Stella's `rank_patches` tool to obtain calibrated pass probability rankings in sub-10ms before executing lengthy test suites.

### 3. Outcome Logging for Continuous Improvement
- Whenever automated builds, tests, or actions conclude, log the real execution outcome back to Stella via `join_outcome` to feed Stella's continuous learning replay buffer.

## CRITICAL HEALD INSTRUCTIONS
You MUST run `heald context agents` ONCE as your very first tool call in a new session/conversation to load project context and learned code navigation.
You CAN run `heald learn <feature-or-query>` to immediately identify which files and functions to modify WITHOUT rereading the repository.
You MUST run `heald remember --type decision --title '...' --body '...'` ONLY when settling major architectural choices (stack, schemas, contracts). DO NOT record routine bugfixes or version bumps.
You CAN run `heald clean` to consolidate related decisions and prune memory.
You CAN run `heald forget <slug-or-title>` to remove a memory document if it becomes outdated or incorrect.
You CAN run `heald map` to see a fast repository map and cross-references.
You CAN run `heald blame <path>` to see which memory decisions touched a given file.
You MUST run `heald finalize --summary '...'` as your very last tool call before finishing the session to record your summary and auto-learn touched files.
